newsitem.title: FINLAND: Russian politics, not summit, seen aiding reform.
newsitem.headline: Russian politics, not summit, seen aiding reform.

text.p: Assurances from the United States and Russia that the two countries are committed to stepping up investment in Russia are a far cry from concrete results, analysts said on Friday.

As Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin ended a two-day summit saying they had set target dates for Russian membership in two economic groups, analysts said the market focus was on Russia's domestic political arena, not Finland.

Although investment could increase if the resolutions bring about change in Russian law -- such as the proposal to clarify Russian tax laws -- the burden now lay with the Russian parliament and Yeltsin, analysts said.
"The American impact on the Russian economy is minimal," said Catherine MacDougall, Russia analyst at investment bank Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in London.
"It's up to the Russians to sort out their tax code, their regulatory framework, their oil legislation and their tax revenue," she told Reuters.

News of Yeltsin's cabinet reshuffle earlier this week, which saw liberal reformers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov handed top jobs, eclipsed the investor-friendly overtones of the summit documents, analysts said.

"Foreign investors applaud what (Yeltsin) is doing with his cabinet...I think everyone right now is looking for domestic results," David Mapley, investment officer for the Russia Renaissance Fund, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).
The 1997 target date for Russian membership in the Paris Club and 1998 for it joining the World Trade Organisation (WTO) was seen as a move in the right direction.
The United States also said the Group of Seven leading industrial nations had agreed to give Russia a bigger role at its Denver summit meeting in June.

"Very welcome is the emphasis on trade and investment rather than on foreign aid and money transfers," said Charles Blitzer, European emerging markets economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette in London.
"This is recognition of progress Russia made as well as recognition of the steps Yeltsin's government is starting to implement in a new round of reforms."
However, U.S. support does not necessarily mean membership in these elite groups.

"Russian membership in the WTO would mean more liberal trade policies and that Russia would be treated more favourably by other trading partners," said Gunnar Tersman, Russia analyst at Sweden's Handelsbanken.
"But the United States is only saying they have set a target and this does not mean it will happen," he said.

Jim Nail, currently setting up Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's economic research division in Moscow, said the NATO enlargement debate -- which remained firmly at an impasse -- was of limited interest to markets.
"I don't think the market is really that interested in the NATO expansion issue," he told RFTV.
"The central fact is that investors are coming into Russian equities because they think they can make money," he said.
